ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: Consider a linear, time-invariant system whose unit-sample response \( h[n] \) is shown in the image. Is it possible to represent this system with a finite number of poles?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The unit sample response given in the figure is h[n] = (1/2)^(n/2), which holds when n = 0, 2, 4, 6, ...; at other n it is 0. The discrete sequence plot below also shows that only nonnegative even positions have nonzero samples, with amplitudes in order of 1, 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, 1/32, ..., that is, decaying by a factor of 1/2 every two sampling points. Reasoning: Let n = 2k, then h[2k] = (1/2)^k, k = 0, 1, 2, .... Therefore the system function H(z) = sum_{k=0}^∞ (1/2)^k z^(-2k). This is a geometric series, and summing gives H(z) = 1 / (1 - (1/2)z^(-2)) = z^2 / (z^2 - 1/2). The denominator z^2 - 1/2 = 0 has two roots z = ±1/sqrt(2), so there are only a finite number of poles.

method.method_draft: First describe the plotted response: samples occur only at even nonnegative indices and decay geometrically by a factor of 1/2 every two samples. Write H(z)=sum_{k=0}^∞ (1/2)^k z^{-2k}. Sum the geometric series to get H(z)=1/(1-(1/2)z^{-2}). The denominator has only two roots, z=±1/sqrt(2), so the system can be represented with a finite number of poles. Answer yes.

method.method_draft: First describe the image pattern: the impulse response alternates zeros at odd n with a decaying geometric subsequence at even n. Observe the recurrence h[n]-(1/2)h[n-2]=0 after the initial impulse, with h[0]=1 and odd samples forced to zero by the two-sample structure. This is realizable by a finite-order feedback relation, e.g. a denominator factor 1-(1/2)z^{-2}. A finite-order denominator implies finitely many poles, specifically two possible pole locations. Therefore the answer is yes.
